claim: Silverstein has said in multiple interviews that on the morning of September 11, 2001 he was at a dermatologist appointment at his wife's insistence, missing his customary breakfast at Windows on the World atop the North Tower. His own account: "So that morning, I was dressing to get downtown to meet with one of the tenants, and my wife said: 'You can't go.' And I said: 'Why? I have an appointment downtown.' She said: 'Because I made an appointment for you with a dermatologist, and that's something you canceled last month and you cannot cancel again.'" Two of his children were not away from the complex that morning. Roger and Lisa Silverstein both worked for Silverstein Properties in temporary offices on the 88th floor of the North Tower, were running late, and reached his Midtown office on foot hours later covered in dust; he did not know whether they had survived until then. The account rests on Silverstein's own telling. No contemporaneous medical or appointment record has been published, and the story does not appear in print until well after the fact: the earliest located accounts are a New York Observer piece of March 17, 2003, The Real Deal in January 2004, and New York Magazine on April 18, 2005 — the first of them roughly eighteen months after the attacks. A late first appearance is a limit on the sourcing, not evidence about the appointment.

notes: Silverstein's dermatologist-appointment account has been told by him in multiple interviews over the years; not a contested fact but an autobiographical claim by him. Cited here as a public statement by Silverstein, not as independent corroboration of his location. Primary would be a video interview where he says it; pending. Expanded 2026-08-22: the record previously carried only the appointment, which is the half that supports a foreknowledge reading. Roger and Lisa Silverstein worked on the 88th floor of the North Tower and were in the building's orbit that morning; that is on the record too and belongs in the same card. Status stays primary-link-pending because the appointment is sourced entirely to Silverstein's own retelling — the upgrade is a contemporaneous record, which has not been published. Provenance checked 2026-08-22 on a bounded search of 2001-2002 coverage: nothing contemporaneous surfaced. The earliest published accounts located are New York Observer 3/17/2003, The Real Deal 1/2004 and New York Magazine 4/18/2005. That is now stated in the card, together with the sentence saying what it does and does not mean — a story that first appears eighteen months later is thinly sourced, and thin sourcing is not evidence of anything in particular. Absence of a 2001 report is unsurprising for a detail about a developer's morning that only became interesting once the foreknowledge argument existed, and the record declines to treat the gap as a finding. Stays primary-link-pending; the upgrade remains a contemporaneous record.
